This is also why dogs were domesticated earlier than cats. Dogs are useful to hunters, and cats are useful to get rid of pests within a territory.

As has already been hinted at, humans never domesticated cats. Cats domesticated themselves willingly because they were intelligent enough to see the benefits of the situation. That being said, it should be noted that while dogs have been domesticated *and* tamed, describing cats as tame is a bit of a stretch.

I daily have moments watching the expression of my cat and get behaviour and I can tell that she regularly switches between a state of self-control and state of pure instinct. The kind of instinct that leads to behaviours such as, "Why were you grooming me a second ago and now you're trying to rip my hair out with your claws and teeth?" Or, "You came to me for pets, but a split second later you're chewing on me?"

It's a simplification to say that these behaviours are simply wild and driven purely by instinct, but they are very heavily *inspired* by instinct, and though dogs also have many instinctual behaviours, cats have actually changed genetically somewhere from very little to not at all in the time that they have been domesticated (I'm sure they have changed, but very little of that change is to do with human direction outside of examples of certain purebreds, and even then many purebred cats are bred less with an inherited predisposition toward humans rather than for other qualities, cats already just happen to get along with [most] people well).

My point being, my cat has all the makings of a wild animal, she just often exhibits enough self-control to not be driven purely by instinct, but rather in tandem. If humans hadn't grown so out of touch with their natural selves, many (more) of us would have more in common with cats. But we not only domesticated dogs, we at some point domesticated ourselves.
